title: Detection Strategy for Impersonation
summary: This strategy detects impersonation, where an adversary presents itself as a trusted person, brand, or internal system in order to obtain access, credentials, or payment. Because the identity being imitated is genuine, detection cannot rely on hostile content; it relies on inconsistencies in the presentation itself. The telemetry that makes this possible is mail gateway records carrying envelope sender, display name, reply to address and authentication results, domain registration or passive DNS feeds showing freshly created lookalike names, identity provider sign in logs carrying application and client agent details, and service desk records for account recovery. It fails in practice because a well written message from a first time external sender is unremarkable on its own, so the rule has to score several weak signals together rather than alert on any single one.

beginner.definition: Impersonation means an attacker pretends to be someone you trust. They may copy a colleague name, a company brand, or the support desk. The goal is to make you act without stopping to check. You may open a file, approve a payment, or hand over a password. This detection looks for signs that the sender is not who they claim to be.
beginner.whyItMatters: The message or the call carries no harmful file, so virus scanning will not help you here. The target is a human decision, and one successful call can cost more than many technical intrusions. Attackers reuse the same tricks many times, so real patterns do exist in the data. Catching the fake identity early protects both your money and your accounts.
howItWorks: The mail gateway stores a record of each message it handles. The record holds the sender address, the display name, the reply to address and the authentication results.
The rule compares the display name and the domain with your trusted list. That list holds internal people, brands and partner organisations.
It looks for failures in the sender authentication checks. Those checks are meant to prove a message came from the domain it claims.
A domain feed tells you whether the sending domain was registered very recently or closely copies a trusted name.
Sign in records are checked for a browser login to a sensitive application from an unfamiliar place.
The service desk queue is checked for a password or multi factor reset that matches the same name or mailbox.
beginner.example: Imagine a stranger phones your reception desk and says they are from head office. They know your manager's name, and they use all the right words. Reception cannot see a face through a phone, so it checks other things. Did the call come from the usual number, and does the request match the normal process? When several answers are wrong, reception calls back on a number the company already trusts.
takeaways: You stop impersonation by checking identity, not by scanning a message for harmful files.
One weak signal means very little, so combine several before you raise an alert.
Always confirm unusual requests through a channel you already trust.

objectives: Describe how impersonation differs from a technical account compromise.
Read mail authentication results and explain what a failure does and does not prove.
Correlate lookalike domain data with inbound mail and identity sign in records.
Recognise account recovery requests that belong to an impersonation campaign.
Design a scoring rule that combines weak signals into a single ranked alert.
dataSources: Mail gateway logs with envelope sender, header from address, display name, reply to address and authentication results for the sending domain
Domain registration or passive DNS feeds showing newly created domains that resemble the organisation or its partners
Identity provider sign in logs with the application name, client user agent, source address and authentication result
Service desk or ticketing records for password reset, multi factor reset and account recovery requests
logic: The pattern is a set of small inconsistencies in how a sender or caller presents a trusted identity, rather than the presence of hostile content anywhere in the message. The fields to correlate are the display name and header from address against the envelope sender in mail records, the authentication results for the sending domain, the age and naming of that domain from registration or passive DNS data, and the application, user agent and source address in identity sign in records for the account being imitated or targeted. The benign case is a legitimate first contact from a real new supplier, where authentication passes, the domain is old enough to be a normal business, and the request arrives through a documented procurement or onboarding process. The malicious case combines a failed or missing authentication result with a freshly registered lookalike domain, a display name that matches an executive or the support desk, and a request for payment details, credentials, or a multi factor reset that appears in the service desk queue.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Inbound Mail With Failed Authentication and Lookalike Display Name
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     dmarc_result: 'fail'
#     spf_result: 'fail'
#     display_name|contains:
#       - 'IT Support'
#       - 'Helpdesk'
#       - 'Finance'
#   filter:
#     sender_domain|endswith: '@approved-partner.example'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: Legitimate bulk mail sent through a third party marketing platform that does not align with the sending domain and so fails authentication.
A real new supplier whose domain was registered recently and whose display name happens to match an internal team.
Messages forwarded through a mailing list or an internal relay, where the forwarding step breaks the authentication result.
Helpful staff who set a display name that matches a shared team mailbox instead of using their own name.
tuningNotes: Score the signals instead of alerting on one: keep a failed authentication result alone at low severity, and let a failure combined with a recently registered domain, a mismatched reply to address, or a display name that matches an executive reach high severity. Filter the bulk mail platforms, mailing lists and forwarding relays you already know about, and keep the watched display name list short and specific so ordinary names never match. Measure how much unauthenticated mail your organisation receives each week before you tune, because tenants with legacy senders will otherwise flood the queue. Combining signals this way loses a narrowly written message that spoofs one internal name accurately and passes authentication through a compromised partner domain, so also watch for replies that move the conversation to a free mail service.
